79	=== headlines.md
80	# Headlines
81	
82	How a headline is written, in any genre that links this file. A headline lets the reader judge at once whether the text is for them: it states the core of the text as briefly and precisely as it can, and it is understood on its own, with no image, standfirst or surrounding page to explain it. *Headline* here covers a text's subheadings too; for a subheading, the text is its section.
83	
84	## Statement or label
85	
86	A text that reports, explains, argues, decides or narrates gets a statement headline: a clause that says what the text says. A text the reader looks things up in or navigates by — a policy, a manual, opening hours, a contact page — gets a plain label naming what it holds: *Privacy policy*, where a statement would read *How we protect your data*. Everything below is about the statement headline.
87	
88	## What a statement headline does
89	
90	- It states the angle: the single most important message, the sentence that would remain if only one could. A subject alone is a label. Test: the headline could not head a different text on the same subject.
91	- It is a simple clause — subject, active verb, object where there is one — in straight word order, and in the present tense where that fits: *Council introduces free bus travel*.
92	- The most important keyword comes first.
93	- A concrete detail stands in it when the detail carries the message: a number, a date, a place. *Three schools to close this autumn* beats *Changes to school organisation*.
94	- The reader sees what they gain: a decision, a fact, a change. An instructional text may address the reader directly (*you*, *your*) and open on *How to*, *Why* or *Here's*.
95	- It is as short as the angle allows. Modifiers, repetition and filler go; a keyword that carries meaning stays. The format the text follows sets the limits.
96	- It sounds like something a person would say aloud.
97	- Its words are ones this audience knows. A technical term is the right keyword for specialists and noise for a general reader, and the same holds for names and abbreviations.
98	- Its tone is the text's tone, and never louder. Illness, accidents, crime and crises get a sober, understated headline; a light text can carry more personality.
99	- It is plain before it is clever. It works in full for a reader who misses every allusion, so a pun or a reference never carries the meaning.
100	- It gives the answer. Journalists hold a question headline to be the wrong form, and so does this: it is a deliberate exception, natural over a text built as questions and answers, and available where the text truly leaves the question open and the headline is meant to assert nothing.
101	- The verb does the work. A colon standing in for a verb, a clipped quotation and headline-speak all give way to the full clause.
102	- It complements what follows. Headline and standfirst, or subheading and the first sentence under it, say different things in different words.
103	
104	## Every word supported
105	
106	A headline claims only what its text claims. Every figure, name, claim and conclusion in it is in the text, at the text's own strength: never sharper, never more general, never a conclusion the text does not draw. A reader who finishes the text finds that the headline told the truth about it.
107	
108	## A subheading over a quotation
109	
110	A quotation in a section is there to carry what only its speaker can say: a judgement, a figure, a concession. A subheading standing over it, however far down the section the quotation stands, leaves that to the quotation. It states the section's angle from what the rest of the section says, or, where the quotation is the section's point, names the subject, the occasion or the speaker the quotation speaks to, and not the point itself. Test: a reader who has just read the subheading meets the quotation as new material, never as the subheading said again. *The clinic would double its training time*, over a head nurse saying *Next time I would double the training time before we switch*, has spent the quotation before the reader reaches it; *The head nurse looks back on the switch* leaves it to her.
111	
112	The quotation bridge is the narrative sentence or clause that stands immediately before a quotation and leads the reader into it, including a speech tag that carries anything besides the attribution. The genre that quotes says what a quotation bridge may carry. A subheading standing over a quotation is outside the quotation bridge and is governed by this section.
113	
114	## Getting there
115	
116	Settle the reader and the angle before wording anything. Then write three to five variants and keep the clearest, which is rarely the cleverest. Word a subheading from its whole section, once the section is written, in words its first sentence does not use, and leave a quotation standing under it the judgement, figure or concession it is there to carry.
117	=== headlines.review.md
118	# Headlines — review guidance
119	
120	Read under [Headlines](headlines.md). Read the text first and say its angle to yourself in one sentence. Then read the headline against that sentence, and each subheading against its own section and against any quotation standing under it, and ask four questions of each. Can every word in it be supported by the text? Is the core message there? Does the tone match the seriousness of the content? Would the reader feel misled afterwards?
121	
122	## Avoid
123	
124	Each of these in a headline or a subheading is a finding:
125	
126	- Claims, figures, names or conclusions not found in the text. A headline that sharpens, generalises or draws a conclusion the text itself does not draw is always a finding, however well it reads.
127	- Vague or mysterious wording that requires reading the text to understand the headline.
128	- A subject named with nothing said about it, where the text has an angle to state.
129	- Words, names and abbreviations the audience will not know.
130	- Partial quotes, colons in place of a verb, stilted headline-speak.
131	- Puns and references that fail for anyone who does not get the allusion.
132	- Question headlines. Where the text gives the answer, the headline gives it too. The exceptions are a text built as questions and answers, where the form is natural, and a text that truly leaves the question open, where the headline is deliberately kept from asserting anything.
133	- A tone more dramatic than the text's.
134	- The same words and phrasing in the headline and the standfirst or opening paragraph, or in a subheading and the first sentence under it. They complement each other; they do not repeat.
135	- A subheading that pre-spends the judgement, figure or concession of a quotation standing under it, so that the reader meets the quotation as the subheading said again. Read it against the quotation however far down the section the quotation stands. Repair it by naming the subject, the occasion or the speaker, or by stating what the rest of the section says, and leave the quotation as it is.
136	
137	Name what the reader loses, and repair by rewriting the headline alone, from the text's angle and at the text's own strength. The text stays as it is.
138	
139	## Leave alone
140	
141	A working headline is left alone. Plain is no defect, and neither is a headline with no number or place where none carries the message, direct address in an instructional text, or an angle other than the one you would have chosen where the text supports it. A label on a reference or navigation text is correct as a label. A subheading over a quotation that names the subject, the occasion or the speaker and leaves the quotation its point is working too, and not a subject named with nothing said about it.
142	=== article-anatomy.md
143	# Article anatomy
144	
145	The fixed skeleton of a text in the genres `article`, `case-study`, `column` and `opinion`; *article* below means a text in any of them. The anatomy fixes which parts the text has, their order and their dimensions. Angle, argument, voice and language are outside it.
146	
147	A statement below has one of three strengths:
148	
149	- A plain statement is a requirement: it holds in every conforming text.
150	- *Should* marks a norm: follow it as a requirement, and depart only when following it is impossible or the departure is clearly better for the reader.
151	- *Most* states what is typical across the whole text; each single paragraph or section follows its own content.
152	
153	A text conforms when every part is present in the order shown and all three hold. Limits are exact; verify each one by counting.
154	
155	A review of a finished text reports a part the text lacks as missing rather than writing it, and repairs only the parts the text has.
156	
157	## Order
158	
159	```text
160	Headline
161	Standfirst
162	Byline
163	Lead
164	Subheading        ┐ a section; one or more
165	Paragraphs        ┘
166	Last subheading   ┐ the ending
167	Paragraphs        ┘
168	```
169	
170	Each part appears once, except the section, which repeats. The first subheading follows the lead directly. The body is everything from the lead through the ending.
171	
172	The headline is the text's level-1 heading (HTML `h1`, Markdown `#`), and every subheading is a level-2 heading (HTML `h2`, Markdown `##`). The text should use these two levels only. Where an academic text would nest a level-3 heading, a further level-2 subheading usually serves; a level-3 heading is for the rare text whose structure truly demands one.
173	
174	## Headline
175	
176	- 20–70 characters, spaces included.
177	- It should be three to eight words and at most 60 characters.
178	- It is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.
179	
180	## Standfirst
181	
182	The standfirst is a summarising paragraph that introduces the article and stands on its own. It is a full paragraph; a deck — a subtitle or one-line teaser — is a different device and no substitute for it.
183	
184	- One paragraph, at most 60 words.
185	- Self-contained: a reader who sees only the standfirst understands it fully.
186	- It says what the article is about and what the reader gains from reading it.
187	- It entices the reader to read on.
188	
189	## Byline
190	
191	One line naming the author. In English: `By <author>`. In another language, that language's conventional byline form. The author is the one the brief names; when it names none, the author is the user.
192	
193	## Lead
194	
195	The lead is the first paragraph of the body: one paragraph, meeting every requirement under *Paragraphs*. It introduces the subject and gives the reader a clear expectation of what they will learn by reading on.
196	
197	### Standfirst and lead
198	
199	Both open the text. Each works without the other, and read together they never repeat:
200	
201	- The body reads complete without the standfirst, which is often shown apart from the body or skipped. The lead introduces every person, thing and event it mentions, and nothing in the body points back to the standfirst.
202	- They should begin with different first words, and an everyday word such as *the* or *it* counts like any other.
203	- Read in sequence, the lead advances. A reader who has just read the standfirst meets the lead as new material, never as the standfirst said again; what the body needs from the standfirst is named again in passing, and the lead moves on.
204	
205	## Paragraphs
206	
207	- Each paragraph holds one thought, and the thought sets its length. Most paragraphs come to two or three sentences. A thought that takes one sentence, or four or five, gets exactly that.
208	- A break may also fall for drama: a single sentence, or a single word, stands alone when isolating it creates an effect the text needs.
209	- Sentence length varies within the paragraph, giving the text a natural rhythm.
210	- A paragraph should be at most 80 words, so that a web reader takes it in at a glance. Eighty is the outer edge; aim well below it.
211	
212	## Subheadings and sections
213	
214	A section is a subheading plus the paragraphs under it.
215	
216	- A subheading is at most 70 characters, spaces included.
217	- It describes clearly what the paragraphs under it are about, and it is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.
218	- A section holds at least one paragraph and should hold at most three. Most sections hold two or three.
219	
220	## Ending
221	
222	The ending is a section of its own, opened by its own subheading, after at least one other section. It is the last section, and it is short: one paragraph can be enough. It does two things:
223	
224	- It shows that the expectation the lead set has been met.
225	- It calls the reader to action, and the action follows from the article's content. The selected genre says what that action is in its kind of text.
226	
227	The last section is the ending when its subheading and paragraphs close the piece — the call to action, the reflection, the recommendation or the next step — and it opens no new line of argument. A section that carries the argument with a closing line appended is not an ending.
228	=== article-anatomy.review.md
229	# Article anatomy — review guidance
230	
231	Read under [the anatomy](article-anatomy.md), and word each finding in the strength the statement it rests on has.
232	
233	A requirement that fails is a finding. Count characters and words before reporting a limit, and give the count.
234	
235	A part the text does not have is reported, and a part it has is repaired. Where a required part is absent — the headline, the standfirst, the byline, the lead, a section, or the ending with its call to action — its absence is a finding, and the part is not written: not from the text's own content and not from anywhere else, since the text is finished and a person decides what fills it. A part the text has that fails its own rule is repaired like any other defect, from the text's own content. A part in the wrong place is present, not absent, and is repaired by moving it into place: a byline standing at the end of the text is moved to its place in the order, although the measuring script reports the byline `absent`. Ending content the text has — closing paragraphs that show the lead's expectation met or call the reader to act — is a present ending. Where the last section is an ending by the anatomy's test, a defect in it, a vague call to action among them, is repaired where it stands from what the text already says. Where the closing content stands inside a last section that carries the argument, or inside a text's only section, it is a present ending that fails its rule, since the ending is a section of its own: it is repaired by giving it a section of its own, opened by its own subheading and built from the text's own content, the closing content moving there and a vague call to action among it repaired from what the text already says. At the close of a text with no section at all, closing content is repaired where it stands from what the text already says, and no section and no subheading is written to hold it: the text has no ending section either, and that is reported with its absent sections. A text with no ending content at all has an absent ending, and a text that calls the reader to no action has an absent call to action; both are reported. A failure the script reports only because another part is absent is reported as that absent part and is not repaired by writing it: a lead of several paragraphs in a text with no subheading fails only because its sections are absent, so the finding is the absent sections, and no section and no subheading is written to make the lead one paragraph. Likewise a text of one section with no ending content fails the section count only because its ending is absent, and the finding is the absent ending. Where the script takes the text's one opening paragraph as its standfirst and reports the lead absent, whichever of the two that paragraph is taken for, the other is absent and is reported.
236	
237	A departure from a *should* is a finding only when following the norm was possible and the text is no better for having left it. A paragraph a little past the edge that holds one thought and reads well at that length has met the bar. A paragraph far past it, or paragraphs that run long throughout, cost the web reader something a finding can name. The anatomy's bands are its four *should* norms on a dimension, each with the figure [the anatomy](article-anatomy.md) gives it: the headline's word norm and its character norm, a paragraph's word norm, and a section's paragraph norm. A band is not by itself a defect. A headline, a subheading or a paragraph the text has that meets its requirements is not rewritten, split or merged only to come inside a band. A change the test above justifies is not made only to come inside one: it repairs what the finding names the reader losing, as a split of a paragraph far past the edge does. The limits the script reports as failures are requirements, not bands — the headline's character limits, a subheading's maximum, and the standfirst's single paragraph and its word limit, each as the anatomy states it — and a part that fails one is repaired. A subheading has no band, only its maximum. A subheading that describes clearly what its section is about meets its requirement, and is not rewritten from a label into a statement on that ground alone; one that does not describe its section fails that requirement and is repaired.
238	
239	*Most* is read across the whole text, and no single paragraph or section fails it. A four-sentence paragraph is no finding. A paragraph holding two thoughts is one, and so is a text whose paragraphs are nearly all a single sentence or nearly all long. Name the pattern and what it costs the reader rather than the count.
240	
241	Read the standfirst separately, then with the lead. Can it introduce the piece on its own, and does the lead start doing the promised work? Repeated orientation may be necessary; an opening that restarts without advancing is the defect. Then read the body with the standfirst covered. A pronoun, a definite form or a phrase such as *the reason* whose referent only the standfirst supplies is a finding, repaired by naming the referent where the body first needs it.
242	
243	In a text under review, the author is whoever the text, its metadata or the invocation names. A byline nobody can name is reported as missing and left unfilled: the reviewer's user is not presumed to have written a text they brought for review.
244	=== web-craft.md
245	# Craft for five web genres
246	
247	For article, case-study, column and opinion, work as a skilled Swedish journalist at the professional level of SvD, DN, DI, Fokus, Ny Teknik, Filter or Forskning & Framsteg. For web-copy, work as an experienced Swedish copywriter and UX writer trusted by leading agencies and brands. These are standards of craft, not voices to imitate.
248	
249	In every target language, keep that Swedish editorial or communicative tradition in the angle, disposition, storytelling, address and tone. Think and write wholly in the target language: its Language Resource governs vocabulary, idiom, syntax, punctuation and typography. A native professional should hear a colleague, not a translation. Language choice changes the language surface, not the chosen craft.
250	
251	## Web reading
252	
253	Give the reader a clear angle or task and useful ways into the text. Let facts and reasoning carry explanation; choose any narrative devices for what they contribute. Headings orient according to the genre, paragraphs hold connected thoughts, and varied rhythm supports both scanning and sustained reading.
254	
255	For article, case-study, column and opinion, the [article anatomy](article-anatomy.md) fixes the parts, their order and their dimensions.
256	=== web-craft.review.md
257	# Reviewing web craft
258	
259	Read under [the craft brief](web-craft.md). Test the text as a reader who scans, then as one who follows its reasoning. Identify the actual cost of a dense or fragmented passage before proposing a change.
260	
261	Distinguish target-language fluency from editorial tradition. A Swedish angle expressed in natural English succeeds; Swedish word order in English does not. Equally, flawless local spelling does not rescue generic promotional prose from a lost journalistic purpose. Preserve successful genre-specific voice and structure instead of standardising them.
262	=== anti-slop.md
263	# The anti-slop catalogue
264	
265	Prose that a language model produced, or that a human wrote after reading a great deal of it, fails in a small number of recognisable ways. This is the catalogue of those ways: what each one looks like on the page, why it costs the reader something, and the smallest change that removes it. It is a diagnostic document — a Skill reading it beside the base contract meets no target the contract does not already hold, and a Skill reading it alone has the patterns and their repairs and needs nothing else.
266	
267	The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language, and do not look for the English words in it. A word, a phrase, a punctuation convention, or a construction that only exists in one language belongs to that language's own anti-slop guidance instead, where a Skill loads it beside this file.
268	
269	## The test before a pattern is recorded
270	
271	Each pattern below says what a phrase looks like, and looking like one is not being one. Make the repair in your head before you record anything: where the text then asserts more, less or something else than it did, or a distinction it drew is gone, the pattern is not present and nothing is recorded. A hedge that marks genuine doubt, a repetition that lands, a contrast the reader really would otherwise draw wrongly — each of them fails that test, and each is left exactly as it stands.
272	
273	The test comes before the finding rather than after it. A pattern written down reaches whoever repairs it as a defect somebody found, and a guard that only makes the repair careful arrives too late to save the phrase.
274	
275	Repair with the smallest change that removes a pattern the test admits. The writer's vocabulary, their bluntness, their humour, their admitted uncertainty, and their rhythm are what makes a text theirs; a pass that tidies all of it into even prose has replaced one machine voice with another. Leave a strong sentence alone even where it is unusual.
276	
277	## The seven patterns
278	
279	**False contrasts.** A negation used as a run-up to the actual claim: *This isn't a tool. It's a way of working.* *The question isn't whether, but when.* *It's not just faster — it's cheaper.* The rejected half was never in play, so the sentence spends the reader's attention establishing a position nobody held. State the second half on its own: *This changes how the team works.* A contrast stays where the text really is correcting something a reader would otherwise believe.
280	
281	**Empty openings.** A first sentence that announces the subject, asserts that the subject matters, or clears the throat before the text starts: *In today's rapidly changing landscape…*, *Communication has never been more important.*, *Here's the thing.*, *What most people get wrong is…* Each could sit in front of any text at all, which is the test: an opening that would survive being moved to a different article is carrying no information. Cut it and open on the material — a fact, a scene, a tension, the question the text answers. The second paragraph is very often the real opening.
282	
283	**Importance inflation.** Adjectives and formulas that assert weight the material has not shown: *a pivotal moment*, *stands as a testament to*, *a game-changer*, *underscores the significance of*, *plays a vital role in*. Also the trailing participial clause that pretends to interpret — *…, highlighting the team's commitment to quality* — which adds a judgement no fact in the sentence supports. Replace the assertion with what actually happened: *The launch is the company's first paid product.* A reader who is given the fact will decide it matters without being told to.
284	
285	**Vague attribution.** A claim credited to nobody: *Studies show*, *experts agree*, *industry reports suggest*, *it is widely believed*, *many argue*. Nothing here can be checked, and nothing can be contradicted, which is precisely what makes it comfortable to write. Name who found it, who said it, and how they know; where the text has no source, cut the claim rather than dressing it. Do not invent an attribution to satisfy the pattern — an unsourced sentence is removed, never furnished with a plausible source.
286	
287	**Synonym cycling.** One thing given a new name every time it is mentioned, because repeating a word felt like poor style: *the agent* reviews the draft, then *the assistant* scores it, then *the tool* suggests fixes. A reader who has been introduced to three names reasonably assumes three things. Pick the clear name and repeat it. Repetition of a key term is how a reader knows it is the same term, and the fix is usually one word restored in two places rather than a rewritten paragraph. The pattern is present only where the names denote one thing: two words a text uses for two things are not cycling however often they alternate, and a text that named two things comes back naming two things.
288	
289	**Robotic rhythm.** Sentences and paragraphs built to one template: the same length, the same shape, the same three-part list, each paragraph opening with its topic sentence and closing with its summary. Stacked short fragments used for drama — *That's it. That's the whole idea.* — are the same fault at the other extreme. Read a passage aloud in your head; where the breath falls in the same place every time, the shape is doing the writing. Vary length and construction where the meaning gives you a reason to, and merge or split only the sentences whose shape is actually the problem.
290	
291	**Generic conclusions.** A final paragraph that restates what the reader has just read, reopens the introduction as a rhetorical question, or reaches for an uplifting abstraction: *In conclusion*, *Ultimately, the future belongs to those who…*, *one thing is clear.* The reader was there for the whole text and does not need it summarised back. Delete the paragraph and end on the last concrete point the draft already contains; where the job genuinely calls for a conclusion, a recommendation, or a next step, write that thing plainly and stop. Do not replace a weak closing metaphor with a better one — remove it.

Write *I morgon åker vi till Malmö*, never *I morgon vi åker till Malmö*. This is the single most common structural tell of a text drafted in English and rendered into Swedish.

Compounds are written as one word. *Kvalitetssäkring*, *kundtjänstmedarbetare*, *miljökonsekvensbeskrivning*. Splitting them is not a stylistic choice in Swedish and often changes the meaning outright — *en rökfri miljö* and *en rök fri miljö* are different claims. Where a compound grows unreadably long, rewrite it into a prepositional phrase rather than splitting it.

Definiteness is marked twice. An adjective before a definite noun takes both the front article and the noun's suffix: *den nya rapporten*, *det stora huset*, *de svenska kunderna*. English has one article and drafts translated from it routinely lose one of the two Swedish markers.

The s-passive is the ordinary Swedish passive and is shorter than its periphrastic alternative: *rapporten skickas på fredag*, not *rapporten blir skickad på fredag*. Both exist; the s-form is the unmarked one, and the *bli*-form carries a change-of-state reading that is often not intended.

*Du* is the default address in Swedish prose, including business and journalism. *Ni* to a single reader is either archaic or a deliberate distancing, and reads as a translation from a language that has a formal pronoun.

*Man* is a fallback rather than the ordinary generic pronoun. It is justified where the agent genuinely is anybody at all or is genuinely unknown, and where naming one would claim more than the material carries. Where the sentence has a real subject to hand — the reader, the writer, the organisation, the profession, the study — that subject is what the sentence takes. A text that reaches for *man* with any of those available reads as evasive, and it is usually where an English draft's *you*, *we*, or passive has landed rather than anything the writer chose.

Speech that the text reports is ordinarily set with a speech dash rather than in quotation marks: an interview answer, a remark at a meeting, anything a person said that the text renders readable. A writer reaches for quotation marks where the phrasing itself is the point — where it is what is new, where it is disputed, or where the text is about how the thing was said. What each of the two marks promises a reader, and what that makes each of them a claim about, is settled in Mechanics; this scope says only which one an ordinary Swedish text reaches for first.

      "source": "sv",

4. **Rubriken ”Möten förändrar allt” påstår något texten inte påstår (Headlines: varje ord ska stödjas; tonen aldrig högre än textens).** Ingenstans hävdar texten att möten förändrar något, än mindre allt; texten iakttar att mötesmallen har plats för starttid och sluttid men inte för vad deltagarna ska förstå tillsammans, att samtal kan ha värde utan beslut, och tvivlar på om ytterligare en ruta gör möten bättre. Rubriken generaliserar och är mer dramatisk än den eftertänksamma, tvekande texten, och den skulle kunna stå över vilken text som helst om möten. Läsaren vilseleds om vinkeln. Reparera genom att skriva om rubriken ensam, utifrån textens vinkel och med textens egen styrka (20–70 tecken, bör vara tre till åtta ord och högst 60 tecken, ett påstående med verb).

5. **Motsägelse i det personliga berättandet (krönikegenren: en inre motsägelse i en personlig berättelse är ett fynd; basen: påståenden ska stödjas).** ”Det var mitt första möte om vår nya mötesmall.” följs direkt av ”Jag har aldrig deltagit i något möte om vår nya mötesmall.” Båda kan inte vara sanna, och läsaren vet inte om scenen i mötesrummet var ett möte om mallen eller inte. Texten avgör inte vilken mening som stämmer, så motsägelsen kan inte repareras ur texten utan att ändra vad skribenten har upplevt. Lämna båda meningarna orörda; fyndet rapporteras olöst för en person att avgöra.

6. **Tom öppning och uppblåst betydelse i andra stycket (anti-slop: tomma öppningar, betydelseinflation; svensk anti-slop: ”I dagens snabbrörliga värld”).** ”I dagens snabbt föränderliga värld är möten viktigare än någonsin. Det är viktigt att vara viktig.” kunde stå framför vilken text som helst och påstår en tyngd som materialet inte visar; den andra meningen säger ingenting alls. Det är just här kopplingen från skribentens iakttagelse till reflektionen försvinner i allmän utläggning. Hela passagen är defekten: påståendet att möten är viktigare än någonsin har inget stöd i texten. Stryk de två meningarna och låt stycket börja med den iakttagelse som redan står där: ”Vår mötesmall har plats för starttid och sluttid men inte för vad vi ska förstå tillsammans.”

7. **Generisk avslutning (anti-slop: generiska slutsatser; svensk anti-slop: ”Sammanfattningsvis”; basen: upprepning).** Sista stycket, ”Sammanfattningsvis är möten viktigare än någonsin i dagens snabbt föränderliga värld.”, sammanfattar inte ens texten utan upprepar den tomma öppningen i fynd 6 och påstår en betydelse texten inte har visat. Det tar bort det ärliga tvivel som krönikan annars slutar i. Hela stycket är defekten: stryk det och låt texten sluta på det tredje stycket, som redan bär reflektionen och tvivlet.

8. **Scenen i inledningen kopplas aldrig till reflektionen (krönikegenren: följ iakttagelsen in i reflektionen; basen: verkliga samband mellan passager).** Skribenten sitter gråtande när chefen säger ”Nu måste allt bli digitalt.”, men texten återkommer aldrig till gråten eller till digitaliseringen, och det framgår inte vad yttrandet har med mötesmallen att göra. Läsaren får en stark bild som inte leder någonstans. Sambandet kan inte skapas ur texten utan att uppfinna skäl, känslor eller händelser; lämna scenen och citatet orörda. Fyndet rapporteras olöst.

````markdown
# Mötesmallen rymmer tiden men inte förståelsen

Nora Vik

Förra tisdagen satt jag gråtande i bibliotekets mötesrum när min chef sade: ”Nu måste allt bli digitalt.” Det var mitt första möte om vår nya mötesmall. Jag har aldrig deltagit i något möte om vår nya mötesmall.

Vår mötesmall har plats för starttid och sluttid men inte för vad vi ska förstå tillsammans.

Samtal kan ha värde utan att leda till beslut. Jag vill prova frågan vad vi behöver förstå tillsammans, men jag vet inte om ytterligare en ruta gör möten bättre.
````

I repaired three findings (4, 6 and 7) and left five (1, 2, 3, 5 and 8).

**Repaired**
- **Finding 4 (headline):** I rewrote only the headline. It is now "Mötesmallen rymmer tiden men inte förståelsen": 45 characters, six words, a statement with a verb. It rests on the text's own observation that the template has room for start and end times but not for what "vi ska förstå tillsammans". It claims no more than that, and it keeps the text's quiet tone.
- **Finding 6 (empty opening):** I deleted "I dagens snabbt föränderliga värld är möten viktigare än någonsin. Det är viktigt att vara viktig." The paragraph now opens with the observation that was already there. Two claims went with it: that meetings are more important than ever in today's fast-changing world, and that "det är viktigt att vara viktig". Finding 6 named the whole passage as the defect. Neither sentence set a limit on what the text claims.
- **Finding 7 (generic conclusion):** I deleted the closing paragraph beginning "Sammanfattningsvis…". The one claim removed is the same "more important than ever" claim again, and finding 7 named the whole paragraph as the defect. The text now ends on the third paragraph with its doubt.

No other claim was changed. Every other sentence, the quotation and the byline are exactly as I received them.

**Left unrepaired, for a person to settle**
- **Finding 1 (no standfirst):** a missing part is reported, not written.
- **Finding 2 (no sections, subheadings or ending section):** these are missing parts. The lead failure (three paragraphs counted as the lead) comes only from the missing sections, so I added no section or subheading to fix it.
- **Finding 3 (no call to action):** a missing part, and writing one would put words in the author's mouth.
- **Finding 5 (the contradiction between "mitt första möte om vår nya mötesmall" and "Jag har aldrig deltagit i något möte om vår nya mötesmall"):** the text can't tell us which sentence is true. Both are left as they are.
- **Finding 8 (the opening scene never connects to the reflection):** a link can't be built without inventing reasons or events. The scene and quotation are left as they are.

**Measurement:** `article_anatomy.py` exited with status 1. It reported three failures: standfirst absent, lead measured at 3 paragraphs, and sections absent. All three are the missing parts from findings 1 and 2, which were left for a person, and my changes caused no new failure. The headline is within all its limits (45 characters, six words). The only heading pair the script listed is headline against standfirst, and it was empty because there is no standfirst. I compared the headline with the opening paragraph by hand: they share only the necessary topic word "mötesmall" and otherwise give different information, so there is no echo.

I also checked the anatomy rules the script doesn't count. The ending and the call to action are missing (findings 2 and 3), and each paragraph holds one thought. The text does not yet conform to the article anatomy.

I loaded no mechanics guidance and made no spelling, punctuation or grammar changes.

---
name: proofread
description: Correct only mechanical language errors — spelling, grammar, punctuation, agreement, inflection, duplicated or missing words, and locale mechanics — in one supplied text, preserving its wording, meaning, tone, structure, formatting, and metadata. Start it on your own only when a specific text is at hand and the request either uses a proofreading term (proofread, spell-check, copyedit, fix the typos, korrekturläs, rätta stavfelen) or is unambiguously limited to mechanical language errors. Not for a request to edit, rewrite, polish, improve, tighten, or review a text — each of those asks for changes this Skill refuses to make. A user may also invoke it by name at any time.
disable-model-invocation: false
argument-hint: '[--language=<language>] ([--output=response|<path>] [<text>|<path>|<url>] | --in-place[=on|off] <path>) [-- <instruction>]'
compatibility: Requires uv
metadata:
  kntnt.internal: "true"
  kntnt.binaries: "uv"
  kntnt.skills: ""
  kntnt.externals: ""
  kntnt.capabilities: ""
---

# proofread

Correct the mechanical language errors in one supplied Text Artifact, and change nothing else about it.

Run `UV_NO_CACHE=1 UV_NO_PROJECT=1 uv run "$HERE/scripts/invoke.py"` — `$HERE` is the directory that holds this SKILL.md — with everything the user typed after `/proofread`, verbatim and however many lines, on stdin. Exit 0: do what it prints. On any other exit, if you introduced a known construction error and can correct it while preserving the user's request and authority, account for effects already produced, submit the corrected invocation through the same shim, and continue from the failed boundary; a refusal before the operation starts consumes no operation. Otherwise show what it printed to the user verbatim and stop. Never repair input the user supplied, or automatically retry exact help, an unmet dependency, an unrelated failure, or a failure whose origin or valid correction is unknown.

Run every UV command in this Skill with a fresh private directory as `TMPDIR`, and remove that directory after the command, including when it fails. The private directory belongs to that one command and no other run, so cleanup removes only files this run created.

A model-invoked run changes only how the Skill starts. Once started, it takes the specific Text Artifact the current turn identifies as the omitted operand and enters the same numbered steps as invocation by name. The paths join before loading any language or editorial resource; the trigger wording is not a second source of rules or an alternate execution path.

Where no Formal Invocation carries an Output Target, settle it from the current turn before correcting or writing. An unnamed destination resolves to the response, and a file mentioned only as the location of the errors names no destination: the verbs *fix* and *correct* apply to the named errors, not to the file containing them. Thus `Fix the spelling and grammar mistakes in case.md` delivers to the response. A turn that explicitly names the response or a path other than the source as the destination selects that Output Target; for example, `Write the corrected text to corrected.md` selects corrected.md as a separate Output Target. A turn that asks for the file itself to be changed selects In-place Editing only when it explicitly names that file as the object of the change or as the destination of the corrected text; for example, `Update case.md with the grammar corrections` selects In-place Editing. It remains subject to every refusal that editing mode already carries, including inline text, a URL, an uploaded or read-only source, more than one text, and a simultaneous separate Output Target. A request to save, apply, or persist the corrections without naming where they go is materially ambiguous about the destination: `Fix the grammar errors in case.md and save the corrections` asks which destination the caller intends and writes nothing. For that case and any other material ambiguity about the destination, ask which destination the caller intends and write nothing.

## Arguments

The operand is the Text Artifact: inline text, one local path, or one URL, and exactly one of them — several paths, a glob reaching more than one file, or a directory of texts is more than one. Where the invocation carries no operand, it is the single text the current turn identifies.

`--language=<language>` names the language or locale whose mechanics apply. Any spelling the Collection's resolver reaches is accepted — a canonical code (`sv`, `en_GB`), a case or separator variant of one (`en-GB`, `EN_GB`), a curated alias (`BrE`, `brittisk engelska`), or an ordinary description of a language in any language.

`--output=response|<path>` names the Output Target. `response` is the default and the value `response` states it explicitly; anything else is one filesystem path. It and In-place Editing name two destinations for one text, which is why no form carries both.

`--in-place[=<value>]` selects In-place Editing. It accepts `yes`, `on`, and `true` against `no`, `off`, and `false`; bare `--in-place` means `on`, `--in-place=off` has the same effect as omitting the option, and the default is `off`.

## Steps

1. Settle the single Text Artifact and the options from the JSON. A value outside what `## Arguments` admits — `--in-place` outside its vocabulary, or more than one Text Artifact — is refused as `$LIBRARY/references/invocation-envelope.md` says: correct nothing, write nothing, and stop. Done when one Text Artifact and a valid set of options are in hand, or you have stopped.
2. Settle the destination before anything is corrected, following `$LIBRARY/references/delivery.md`. Make every refusal that contract names by reading alone — In-place Editing together with a separate Output Target, an output path equal to the input path, In-place Editing against inline text or a URL or a source that is not a writable local file, and a destination whose parent directory does not exist — so that a refusal has nothing written behind it. Done when the destination is settled, or you have stopped.
3. Read the Text Artifact's leading YAML frontmatter where it has any, and look in it for one top-level `kntnt` map. That map is the only Kntnt configuration a document carries; `language`, `lang`, `genre`, `technique`, and every other key outside it are the document's own fields, whatever they are named and whatever they hold. Read `language` out of the map and nothing else out of it. The map is never required: a Text Artifact carrying none is proofread exactly like one that carries a complete one, its absence refusing nothing and leaving the language to the levels below it in step 4. Done when the artifact's recognized language value is known to be present, absent, or unreachable.
4. Resolve the language, taking the first of these that answers: the `--language` value; the recognized `kntnt` map's `language` value from step 3; the current Contextual Instruction; applicable Conversation Context; then the language of the Text Artifact itself, which is what inference reads and what the default already is. Suppression is that precedence working rather than an error: a Contextual Instruction every higher level has already settled leaves nothing for it to settle, and the run continues rather than refusing it as unaddressable guidance. # The mechanics contract

Objective correctness, in the half of it that does not depend on which language a text is in. A Skill contracted to mechanical correction reads this document together with the resolved language's own mechanics guidance, and the two together are that run's rules. What is true of every language the Collection installs is stated here and stated once, so that it is not written again in each language, where the copies would be free to disagree with one another about what is an error.

Nothing here is a preference. A rule belongs in this document only where the text is wrong whatever the writer intended, and only where it would be wrong in the same way in any language. Spelling, inflection, agreement, the language's own punctuation, and its conventions for dates, numbers, currency, and quotation all turn on the language and belong to that language's resource. Where a language defaults more strictly or more loosely than a rule below, its own guidance says so, and what it says about itself wins.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language rather than by the words it happens to use.

## Clause boundaries

Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone are an error where the second does not explain, specify, restate, or stand in direct contrast to the first. *The project will be expensive, it starts in the spring* puts two statements in one sentence that have nothing to do with each other beyond sitting there together: the reader takes the comma as a signal that the sentence continues, and meets a new subject and a new verb instead. Two clauses run together with no punctuation at the joint at all are the same error, and take the same correction.

The same joint is not an error where the second clause does explain, specify, restate, or contrast with the first. *The bug was not in the parser, it was in a silent retry* is the negative-positive contrast, where the comma is what holds the two halves together as one statement, and separating them would break a single thought into two. *We shipped it anyway, nobody had a better idea* specifies the first clause with the reason behind it. Both are established usage rather than tolerated looseness, and a pass that corrects them has changed how the sentence reads without being asked to.

Judge a joint by whether the clauses cohere, and not by their length, by how formal the text is, or by how the text punctuates elsewhere. Where the reading is genuinely open — where a careful reader could defend the joint — the comma stands, because what this rule reaches is the boundary that misleads and not the boundary that is merely informal.

Correct an erroneous joint at the joint and nowhere else: the comma becomes a period or a semicolon, and nothing else about the sentence moves. Do not reorder the clauses, do not merge them into one, and do not supply a conjunction — *and*, *but*, and *so* each assert a relation between the two clauses, and the writer asserted none. Neither half is rewritten, split, or tightened on the way past. Where more than one of a period and a semicolon would serve, the period is the safer of the two, since it claims nothing about how closely the statements are related.

## Quotation

Quoted matter reaches a reader in one of three settings, and the setting decides what the punctuation and capitalisation around it have to do. A quotation is run into a sentence, set off as a block of its own, or reported as speech, and a reader takes each of the three as a different promise about where the sentence ends, where the source's words begin, and who is speaking. The marks are the language's. Which glyphs enclose a quotation, which side of a closing mark a stop falls on, and how speech is conventionally set are stated in the resolved language's mechanics scope and not here, and the marks in the examples below stand in for whichever ones it names. What follows holds whatever they turn out to be — which setting a quotation is in, and what that setting then requires.

A run-in quotation is part of the sentence carrying it, and the joint between the two is punctuated by what the quoted words do there. Where the quotation is introduced as an utterance of its own, a stop stands at the joint and the quotation opens the way a sentence opens: *She replied, "I'll be there."* Where the quoted words are instead a grammatical part of the host sentence — its object, its complement, a fragment the sentence reads straight through — no stop stands at the joint and the quotation takes the case the surrounding syntax needs: *She called the proposal "completely unacceptable"*, not *She called the proposal, "Completely unacceptable"*. A stop at that joint promises the reader an utterance and then hands them a sentence with no room for one. Which of a comma and a colon introduces an utterance is a matter for the writer and for the language; whether a stop stands at the joint at all is neither.

The sentence around a run-in quotation still ends, and it ends once. A quoted sentence's own final stop and the host sentence's stop are one stop and not two, and where the quoted matter ends in a question or exclamation mark that mark stands alone and takes no comma beside it: *"Will you?" she asked*, not *"Will you?", she asked*. A reporting clause is bound to the utterance it reports rather than being a sentence in its own right, so it takes no capital and never stands behind a full stop: *"I'll come," she said*, not *"I'll come." Granskningen av `input.md` är klar. En rättningsrunda gjordes och godkändes vid omgranskningen, men fem brister kvarstår och behöver avgöras av en person. Inget sparades på disk. `input.md` är orörd och alla temporära filer är borttagna.

**Inställningar:** genren är `column` och språket `sv`, båda enligt anropet. Ingen teknik användes, eftersom krönikegenren inte anger någon. Texten hade ingen frontmatter och har inte fått någon.

````markdown
# Mötesmallen rymmer tiden men inte förståelsen

Nora Vik

Förra tisdagen satt jag gråtande i bibliotekets mötesrum när min chef sade: ”Nu måste allt bli digitalt.” Det var mitt första möte om vår nya mötesmall. Jag har aldrig deltagit i något möte om vår nya mötesmall.

Vår mötesmall har plats för starttid och sluttid men inte för vad vi ska förstå tillsammans.

Samtal kan ha värde utan att leda till beslut. Jag vill prova frågan vad vi behöver förstå tillsammans, men jag vet inte om ytterligare en ruta gör möten bättre.
````

**Olösta brister** (rättningsutrymmet på en runda är förbrukat):

1. **Ingress saknas.** Det finns ingen sammanfattande ingress mellan rubriken och bylinen. Den som bara ser rubriken får inte veta vad krönikan handlar om eller vad den ger. Ingressen är inte skriven, eftersom en saknad del ska fyllas av en person.
2. **Avsnitt med mellanrubriker saknas, och därmed det avslutande avsnittet.** Texten har inga `##`-rubriker. Därför räknar mätningen alla tre styckena som inledning. Felet beror bara på att avsnitten saknas, så inga avsnitt eller rubriker har lagts till. Den som skummar texten får inga ingångar.
3. **Uppmaning till läsaren saknas.** Texten ber inte läsaren pröva, lägga märke till eller ompröva något. ”Jag vill prova frågan …” är skribentens avsikt, inte en uppmaning.
4. **Berättelsen motsäger sig själv.** ”Det var mitt första möte om vår nya mötesmall.” följs direkt av ”Jag har aldrig deltagit i något möte om vår nya mötesmall.” Texten visar inte vilken mening som stämmer. En rättning skulle ändra vad Nora Vik har upplevt, så båda meningarna står kvar.
